H1.text: Multiply a plus b by itself, and you get three terms.

H2.text: Multiply it three times, and you get four terms. It already takes a while.

H3.text: Aarav's homework tonight asks for a plus b, to the power ten.

H4.text: Ten brackets, multiplied one by one. That is a whole page of work. Is there a shortcut?

H5.text: There is. One line gives the whole answer. It is called the binomial theorem.

D1.text: Start at the canteen. Three friends each order one drink, tea or coffee.

D2.text: Each friend has two choices, so there are two times two times two, eight different orders.

D3.text: In maths, tea is a and coffee is b. Each friend is one bracket. A plus b, cubed, is just three friends choosing.

P1.text: Now watch all eight orders appear. Tea, tea, tea gives a cubed. Tea, tea, coffee gives a squared b.

P2.text: Now sort them by how many coffees there are.

P3.text: No coffee: one order. One coffee: three orders. Two coffees: three orders. Three coffees: one order.

P4.text: So a plus b, cubed, is a cubed, plus three a squared b, plus three a b squared, plus b cubed.

C1.text: Here is the key question. Why are there exactly three orders with one coffee?

C2.text: Because you only decide who gets the coffee. The first friend, the second, or the third.

C3.text: Choosing r things out of n is n C r, from the combinations episode. Here, three C one is three.

C4.text: So every number in front of a term is an n C r. It counts the ways to choose which brackets give b.

L1.text: Now let the number of friends grow. Watch n count up from one to ten.

L2.text: Each new power adds one more term. The numbers grow fast, and they rise and fall evenly, like a hill.

L3.text: At n equals ten, the numbers add up to one thousand and twenty four. That is two to the ten, because each of ten friends had two choices.

G1.text: Now we can write the theorem in one line.

G2.text: Step one. The first term is a to the n. Nobody picks b, and n C zero is one.

G3.text: Step two. In each next term, one a becomes one b. The power of a goes down by one, and the power of b goes up by one.

G4.text: Step three. In front of a to the n minus r, times b to the r, sits n C r. That is the number of ways to choose r brackets for b.

G5.text: Step four. The last term is b to the n, with n C n, which is also one.

G6.text: So there are n plus one terms. And in every term, the two powers add up to n.

S1.text: Side by side. Many people think a plus b, squared, is just a squared plus b squared.

S2.text: Look at a square with side a plus b. It splits into four pieces. a squared, b squared, and two rectangles, each a times b.

S3.text: So a plus b, squared, is a squared, plus two a b, plus b squared. The middle term is what the shortcut forgets.

S4.text: Now you try. Is a plus b, cubed, equal to a cubed plus b cubed? Pause and decide.

S5.text: No! The middle terms, three a squared b and three a b squared, are missing. Only the first and last terms match.

T1.text: Remember this. Pick one part from every bracket, and n C r counts the ways.

W2.text: Expand x plus two, to the power four.

W3.text: Step one. n is four, so the numbers are four C zero up to four C four. One, four, six, four, one.

W4.text: Step two. The powers of x go down from four to zero. The powers of two go up from zero to four.

W5.text: Step three. Multiply each column. x to the four. Eight x cubed. Twenty four x squared. Thirty two x. Sixteen.

W6.text: Check with x equal to one. Three to the four is eighty one, and one plus eight plus twenty four plus thirty two plus sixteen is also eighty one.

X2.text: Expand x minus two, to the power four. Many students turn every plus into a minus.

X3.text: But only odd powers of minus two are negative. Minus two, squared, is plus four. So the signs alternate: plus, minus, plus, minus, plus.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In JEE Main, as questions on the sum of all the coefficients, which you get by putting x equal to one.

Q1.text: Exam level now. How many terms does this expansion have? Pause and solve.

A2.text: Put x equal to one. The coefficients add up to one plus two, to the power n. That is three to the n.

A3.text: Three to the eight is exactly six thousand five hundred sixty one, so n is eight.

A4.text: There is always one more term than the power. So the expansion has nine terms, not eight.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is a plus b, squared, not just a squared plus b squared?

Y3.text: Two. How many terms does a plus b, to the power seven, have?

Y4.text: Three. What do the coefficients of one plus x, to the power five, add up to?

N1.text: Next time: you need only the seventh term of a long expansion. Can you jump straight to it? We find out with the general term.
